subject: Biology
title: Support and Movement (KPK Board)
learningOutcomes: Define a skeleton and differentiate between cartilage and bone.
Describe the role of the skeleton in support and movement.
Explain that the skeletal system is a dynamic, living tissue capable of growth, that adapts to stress and repairs itself after injury.
Describe the main components of the axial skeleton and the appendicular skeleton.
Describe the contribution of Vesalius in describing the bones and muscles in humans.
Differentiate between movable joints and immovable joints.
State the role of ligaments and tendons.
Describe the location and movement of hinge joints.
Identify ball-and-socket joints in the human body.
Describe the action of flexors and extensors as a pair of opposing muscles, using biceps and triceps as an example.
Describe the effect of calcium deficiency on bones and relate it to osteoporosis.
Discuss the causes, symptoms and treatment of arthritis.
Relate the onset of arthritis with age and weight-bearing joints.

sections.heading: The Skeleton and Locomotion
sections.body: Free movement, also known as locomotion, is a life characteristic of all living animals; it helps them to utilise the environment in the best possible way and to save themselves from predators. The earthworm, a common invertebrate found in the soil, always crawls on the ground and moves slowly, because it does not have any skeleton to support it to stand erect and move faster. All animals which can move fast possess some type of skeleton. A skeleton is the framework of hard structures that provide physical support and protection for the bodies of animals; it also helps in locomotion.

sections.heading: Endoskeleton, Exoskeleton and the Living Skeleton
sections.body: Like other vertebrates, the human skeleton lies inside the body and is called an endoskeleton. The skeletal system of some invertebrates, for example arthropods, is outside the body and is called an exoskeleton. The human skeleton is made of living tissue: it contains living cells and also has nerves and blood vessels. It is a dynamic tissue that can grow, repair itself after injury and adapt to stress.

sections.heading: Role of the Skeletal System
sections.body: The skeleton forms the hard structure of the body and gives it a definite shape. Skeletal muscles are attached to the bones, so the bones can move and thus we can move. The skull protects the brain, the vertebral column protects the spinal cord, and the lungs and heart are protected in the rib cage. The bone marrow produces red blood cells, platelets and white blood cells. Bones store mineral salts such as calcium, potassium and phosphorus, which is why they remain hard and strong. The functions of the skeleton are shape, support, movement, protection and blood cells production, and in different animals the shape of the skeleton is in accordance with the requirement of the particular animal's type.

sections.heading: Parts of the Human Skeleton
sections.body: The human skeleton is composed of two parts: the axial skeleton and the appendicular skeleton. An adult human skeleton has 206 bones, of which the axial skeleton has 80 and the appendicular skeleton has 126. At the time of birth human infants have about 350 bones; as the child grows many of these bones fuse together and their number reduces to 206. The largest bone of the human body is the femur and the smallest bone is found in the internal ear.

sections.heading: The Axial Skeleton: Skull and Vertebral Column
sections.body: The term axis means the central point around which other structures are distributed, and the axial skeleton lies in the centre of the body. It includes the skull, the vertebral column, the ribs and the sternum. The skull is made up of the cranium (8 bones, which protect the brain) and the 14 facial bones, which make the skeletal part of our face. The vertebral column extends from the skull to the pelvis, allows us to stand erect and protects the spinal cord. It consists of 33 vertebrae: 7 cervical vertebrae in the neck, 12 thoracic vertebrae in the chest region, 5 lumbar vertebrae in the back region and 9 pelvic vertebrae, which form two sets, the sacrum (fusion of the anterior five vertebrae) and the coccyx (fusion of four posterior vertebrae).

sections.heading: The Axial Skeleton: Ribs, Sternum and Other Bones
sections.body: There are 12 pairs of ribs, attached on the dorsal (back) side with the vertebrae. Out of these, 10 pairs connect anteriorly with the chest bone (sternum), either directly or through an arch. The rib cage supports the thoracic cavity, in which vital organs like the heart and lungs lie. The lower 2 pairs of ribs are called floating ribs because they do not attach to the sternum. Each human ear has three small bones called ossicles (the malleus, the incus and the stapes), and there is one bone in the neck called the hyoid bone.

sections.heading: The Appendicular Skeleton
sections.body: The appendicular skeleton consists of 126 bones: the pectoral girdle, the forelimbs (arms and hands), the pelvic girdle and the hind limbs (legs and feet). The pectoral girdle attaches the forelimbs to the vertebral column and is comprised of 4 bones of the shoulder (2 on each side). The arms contain 6 bones (3 in each arm) and the hands contain 54 bones (27 in each hand). The pelvic girdle attaches the hind limbs to the vertebral column and consists of 2 bones. The legs contain 8 bones (4 in each leg), while the feet contain 52 bones (26 in each foot).

sections.heading: Bones
sections.body: The human skeleton is made up of two types of connective tissue: bones and cartilage. Bones are the hardest and most rigid form of connective tissue in the body. Muscles pull our bones to enable movements, and bones give shape and structure to the body and protect delicate internal organs. The hard, white outer layer of a bone is the compact bone; its matrix contains collagen fibres and is saturated with calcium phosphate, which gives strength to the bone. Bone cells called osteocytes lie in spaces called lacunae, and the matrix contains nerve fibres and blood vessels that keep the osteocytes alive. Beneath the compact bone is the spongy bone, whose spaces contain bone marrow, where most blood cells are formed.

sections.heading: Cartilage
sections.body: Cartilage is a specialised connective tissue which is firm and flexible and does not stretch. It has great tensile strength and is much softer than bone. In adults, cartilage covers the ends of bones at joints (like the knee joint); it also supports the flexible portion of the nose and the external ears (pinna). Its ground substance is an amorphous gel-like substance containing collagen fibres in parallel arrangements. The cells of cartilage are chondrocytes, which lie in spaces called lacunae, and their number decides how flexible or elastic the cartilage is. There are no blood vessels in the ground substance, and one of its main functions is to keep bones from rubbing together, thus reducing friction. In common words cartilage is called soft bone; in early embryonic life the whole skeleton is made of cartilage, which then gradually turns into bones.

sections.heading: Types of Cartilage
sections.body: There are three types of cartilage. Elastic cartilage has cells closer together with less ground substance and is found in the external ear flaps and the epiglottis. Hyaline cartilage has fewer cells and more ground substance and is found at the ends of long bones and in the nose, ears, trachea, larynx and bronchi. Fibrous cartilage has the least number of cells, and therefore the maximum ground substance, and is found in the inter-vertebral disc.

sections.heading: Joints
sections.body: A joint is formed at the meeting point of two or more bones. Joints keep the bones together, allow the bones to move to different extents and give mobility to the body. On the basis of the extent of movement they allow, joints are classified into three categories. In immovable joints the bones are fused together and do not allow any movement, for example the joints among the bones of the skull. Slightly movable joints allow little movement, for example the joints of the vertebral column and the ribs. Freely movable joints allow free movements.

sections.heading: Hinge and Ball-and-Socket Joints
sections.body: There are two major types of freely movable joints. Hinge joints allow movement only in two directions and are present at the elbow and the knee. Ball-and-socket joints allow movement in all directions (up, down, forward and backward); the hip joint and the shoulder joint are examples of ball-and-socket joints.

sections.heading: Tendons and Ligaments
sections.body: Ligaments are tough bands of connective tissue which hold the bones at the joints in place. Tendons are tough connective tissues which attach muscles to bones. When a muscle contracts, the tendon exerts a pulling force on the attached bone, and as a result the bone is pulled towards the muscle.

sections.heading: Andreas Vesalius (1514-1564)
sections.body: Andreas Vesalius was born in Brussels and was a professor of Anatomy at Padua University in Italy. In 1543 he wrote the first major book on human anatomy, called The Fabric of the Human Body. He worked closely with the famous artist Titian, who produced 277 anatomical illustrations for the book. Vesalius explained the different parts of the human skeleton, including the number of bones, and he also described the source and position of each muscle and provided information on their respective functions.

sections.heading: Muscles and Their Types
sections.body: Locomotion and all other types of movement are due to the contraction of muscles. There are three types of muscles in the body. Cardiac muscle (heart muscle) is an involuntary muscle whose contractions help the heart pump blood throughout the body, and it keeps on contracting throughout life. Smooth muscles are found in the walls of organs such as the digestive tract, air passageways, blood vessels and the urinary bladder; their contractions move materials within the organs. Skeletal muscles are attached to the bones of the skeleton and their contractions help us in movement and locomotion.

sections.heading: Antagonistic Muscles: Biceps and Triceps
sections.body: Skeletal muscles are attached to bones by tendons and are under voluntary control. One end of a skeletal muscle is always attached to a fixed bone (the origin) and the other end to a moving bone (the insertion). Most skeletal muscles are arranged in pairs: when one muscle contracts (pulls), the other relaxes or elongates. The phenomenon in which one muscle opposes the action of the other is called antagonism, and such muscles are antagonistic muscles. Muscles can only pull bones; they cannot push them. When the biceps contracts, its insertion pulls the radius bone upward and the lower arm bends (flexion), so the biceps is the flexor. When the triceps contracts, its insertion pulls the ulna bone back and the lower arm straightens (extension), so the triceps is the extensor.

sections.heading: Osteoporosis
sections.body: The process of mineralisation forms bones: calcium phosphate is deposited in the collagen fibres to make the bones hard, and this calcium is absorbed from the food we eat. When a person does not take sufficient calcium in the daily diet, the bones start becoming weak. Demineralisation is the process in which calcium moves from the bones to the blood in order to maintain the calcium level of the blood. If this situation prolongs, the bones become soft and fragile; this disorder is known as osteoporosis. Such bones start bending and can be broken easily. Osteoporosis occurs especially in old people and in women.

sections.heading: Arthritis
sections.body: Arthritis is the disorder of the joints in which they get inflamed. It is a degenerative disease that damages the joints permanently, causing pain, stiffness and swelling. The membranes lining the joints thicken and fluid production decreases, which increases friction and causes severe pain; in later stages this leads to complete immobility, and the joints become permanently swollen and de-shaped. There are three types of arthritis. Osteoarthritis is the most common type: the cartilage wears away over time, in extreme cases leaving bone-on-bone contact; it occurs most often in older people and usually affects the weight-bearing joints (the joints of the vertebrae, knee and hip). Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks healthy joints and can destroy the cartilage and bone; it usually affects the joints in the fingers, wrists, knees and elbows. Gouty arthritis is caused by higher-than-normal levels of uric acid in the blood, which is deposited in the lining of the joints in the form of crystals; it usually affects the joint at the base of the big toe.

sections.heading: Treatment of Arthritis
sections.body: Treatment of arthritis focuses on relieving symptoms and improving joint function. Analgesics (pain killers) and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are used to treat arthritis. Surgery can also be performed, in which the affected joint is replaced with an artificial joint. Arthroplasty is a surgery that replaces a damaged, worn-out or diseased joint with an artificial joint; most knee replacements are carried out on people between the ages of 60 and 80, and the most common reason is osteoarthritis.

definitions.definition: The framework of hard structures that provide physical support and protection for the bodies of animals.
Free movement of animals, a life characteristic of all living animals.
A skeleton that lies inside the body, as in humans and other vertebrates.
A skeleton present outside the body, as in some invertebrates such as arthropods.
The 80 bones lying in the centre of the body: the skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum.
The 126 bones of the limbs and the pectoral and pelvic girdles.
The 8 bones of the skull that protect the brain.
The backbone of 33 vertebrae extending from the skull to the pelvis; it allows us to stand erect and protects the spinal cord.
The bone formed by the fusion of the anterior five pelvic vertebrae.
The bone formed by the fusion of four posterior pelvic vertebrae.
The lower 2 pairs of ribs, which do not attach to the sternum.
The three small bones in each ear: the malleus, the incus and the stapes.
The 4 bones of the shoulder that attach the forelimbs to the vertebral column.
The 2 bones that attach the hind limbs to the vertebral column.
The hardest and most rigid form of connective tissue in the human body.
The hard, white outer layer of a bone.
The bone layer beneath the compact bone, whose spaces contain bone marrow.
Bone cells that lie in spaces called lacunae in the bone matrix.
A specialised connective tissue which is firm and flexible, does not stretch and is much softer than bone.
The cells of cartilage, which lie in spaces called lacunae in the ground substance.
The meeting point of two or more bones.
A tough band of connective tissue which holds the bones at the joints in place.
A tough connective tissue which attaches a muscle to a bone.
The point where a muscle attaches to the fixed bone.
The point where a muscle attaches to the moving bone.
The phenomenon in which one muscle opposes the action of another muscle.
A muscle whose contraction bends a limb, e.g. the biceps bends the lower arm.
A muscle whose contraction straightens a limb, e.g. the triceps straightens the lower arm.
The process in which calcium phosphate is deposited in the collagen fibres to make the bones hard.
The process in which calcium moves from the bones to the blood in order to maintain the calcium level of the blood.
A disorder in which the bones become soft and fragile due to prolonged calcium deficiency.
A degenerative disorder of the joints in which they get inflamed, causing pain, stiffness and swelling.
The most common type of arthritis, in which the cartilage wears away over time.
An autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks healthy joints.
Arthritis caused by uric acid crystals deposited in the lining of the joints (gout).
A surgery that replaces a damaged, worn-out or diseased joint with an artificial joint.

examTips: Learn the key numbers together: adult skeleton 206 bones = axial 80 + appendicular 126; skull 22 = cranium 8 + facial 14; vertebral column 33 = 7 cervical + 12 thoracic + 5 lumbar + 9 pelvic; 12 pairs of ribs, of which the lower 2 pairs are floating ribs.
Prepare the comparisons as tables: axial vs appendicular skeleton, bone vs cartilage, hinge vs ball-and-socket joint, tendon vs ligament, biceps (flexor) vs triceps (extensor).
Do not mix up the joint types: immovable (skull), slightly movable (vertebral column and ribs), freely movable - hinge (elbow, knee) and ball-and-socket (hip, shoulder).
Remember origin = fixed bone and insertion = moving bone; muscles can only pull, so they work in antagonistic pairs.
Link osteoporosis with calcium: low calcium in the diet leads to demineralisation, so the bones become soft and fragile - and keep it separate from arthritis, which is a disorder of the joints.
Know the three types of arthritis with their cause: osteoarthritis (cartilage wears away with age, weight-bearing joints), rheumatoid arthritis (autoimmune) and gouty arthritis (uric acid crystals).

practiceQuestions.prompt: What is the framework of hard structures that gives physical support and protection to the body of an animal called?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The framework of hard structures that provides physical support and protection for the bodies of animals is called the skeleton.

practiceQuestions.prompt: How many bones are present in an adult human skeleton?
practiceQuestions.explanation: An adult human skeleton has 206 bones.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which tough connective tissues attach muscles to bones?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Tendons are tough connective tissues which attach muscles to bones.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which compound saturates the bone matrix and gives strength to the bone?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The matrix of bone is saturated with calcium phosphate, which gives strength to the bone.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which freely movable joint allows movement in all directions (up, down, forward and backward)?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A ball-and-socket joint allows movement in all directions (up, down, forward and backward).

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which type of cartilage is found in the inter-vertebral disc?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The cartilage found in the inter-vertebral disc is fibrous cartilage.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What is the point where a muscle attaches to the fixed bone called?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The point where the muscle attaches to the fixed bone is called the origin.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which type of arthritis is an autoimmune disease?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease in which the body's immune system attacks healthy joints.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The lower 2 pairs of ribs are called floating ribs because they do not attach to the sternum.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The lower 2 pairs of ribs are called floating ribs because they do not attach to the sternum.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Blood vessels are present in the ground substance of cartilage.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. There are no blood vessels in the ground substance of cartilage.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Hinge joints allow movement in all directions.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Hinge joints allow movement only in two directions; ball-and-socket joints allow movement in all directions.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Muscles can only pull bones; they cannot push them.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Muscles can only pull bones, which is why they work in antagonistic pairs.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The point where the muscle attaches to the moving bone is called the ____.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The point where the muscle attaches to the moving bone is called the insertion.

practiceQuestions.prompt: In demineralisation, calcium moves from the bones to the ____.
practiceQuestions.explanation: In demineralisation, calcium moves from the bones to the blood.

sequencingActivity.prompt: Arrange the events that lead to osteoporosis in the correct order.

items: The bones become soft and fragile
Calcium moves from the bones to the blood
Too little calcium is taken in the daily diet
This situation continues for a long time
correctOrder: Too little calcium is taken in the daily diet
Calcium moves from the bones to the blood
This situation continues for a long time
The bones become soft and fragile

sequencingActivity.explanation: When too little calcium is taken in the diet the bones start becoming weak; calcium moves from the bones to the blood (demineralisation), and if this situation prolongs the bones become soft and fragile, a disorder called osteoporosis.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A girl has taken very little calcium in her diet for many years. Which change is expected in her bones?

options: Calcium moves from the bones to the blood, so the bones become soft and fragile
Calcium moves from the blood to the bones, so the bones become harder
The bones fuse together and their number reduces to 206
The bones change into muscle tissue

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: When the diet lacks calcium, demineralisation moves calcium from the bones to the blood to maintain the calcium level of the blood; if this prolongs, the bones become soft and fragile (osteoporosis).

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Raza can swing his arm in every direction at the shoulder, but at the elbow he can only bend and straighten it. Which types of joints are these?

options: Shoulder: hinge joint; elbow: ball-and-socket joint
Shoulder: ball-and-socket joint; elbow: hinge joint

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint (movement in all directions), while the elbow is a hinge joint (movement only in two directions).

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A student lifts a book and his biceps contracts. What happens to the triceps and to the lower arm?

options: The triceps contracts and the lower arm bends upward
The triceps relaxes and the lower arm straightens
The triceps relaxes and the lower arm bends upward (flexion)
Both muscles contract and the arm stays still

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: The biceps and triceps are antagonistic: when the biceps contracts, its insertion pulls the radius upward, the triceps relaxes and the lower arm bends - this is flexion.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Because muscles can only pull and never push, the biceps and triceps work as an ______ pair of muscles.
bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Muscles can only pull bones, so they work in antagonistic pairs: when one contracts the other relaxes.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: An elderly person has pain in the weight-bearing knee and hip joints because the cartilage is slowly wearing away. This is most likely rheumatoid arthritis.
bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Wearing away of the cartilage in older people, especially in weight-bearing joints such as the knee and hip, is osteoarthritis. Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease that usually affects the fingers, wrists, knees and elbows.
